framework: US NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023)
requirement_paraphrase: AI systems should be tested before deployment and regularly while in operation; measurement should include rigorous software testing and performance assessment with measures of uncertainty, benchmark comparisons and documented reporting of results.
who_tests: AI actors performing TEVV (internal or external)

framework: US NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023)
requirement_paraphrase: Processes for independent review can improve effectiveness of testing and mitigate internal bias and conflicts of interest.

framework: US NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023)
requirement_paraphrase: Select measurement approaches and metrics for the risks identified in MAP, starting with the most significant; document risks or trustworthiness characteristics that will not or cannot be measured; regularly assess appropriateness of metrics and effectiveness of controls.

framework: US NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023)
requirement_paraphrase: Involve internal experts who did not serve as front-line developers and/or independent assessors in regular assessments; consult domain experts, users, external AI actors and affected communities as needed per risk tolerance.
who_tests: Internal non-developer experts and/or independent assessors

framework: US NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023)
requirement_paraphrase: Measure and demonstrate AI system performance or assurance criteria under conditions similar to deployment settings, and document the measures.

framework: US NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023)
requirement_paraphrase: Demonstrate that the system to be deployed is valid and reliable; document limits on generalisability beyond the conditions under which it was developed.

framework: US NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023)
requirement_paraphrase: Evaluate regularly for safety risks; demonstrate that the system to be deployed is safe, residual risk does not exceed tolerance, and it can fail safely, including beyond its knowledge limits.

framework: US NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023)
requirement_paraphrase: Evaluate and document AI system security and resilience as identified in MAP.

framework: US NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023)
requirement_paraphrase: Examine and document transparency/accountability risks; explain, validate and document the model and interpret output in context; examine and document privacy risk.

framework: US NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023)
requirement_paraphrase: Evaluate fairness and bias as identified in MAP and document results.

framework: US NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023)
requirement_paraphrase: Evaluate and document the effectiveness of the TEVV metrics and processes themselves.

framework: US NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023)
requirement_paraphrase: Connect measurement approaches to deployment context with domain-expert consultation; inform results on trustworthiness in deployment context by domain experts and relevant AI actors to validate that the system performs consistently as intended, and document results.

framework: US NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023)
requirement_paraphrase: Make and record a determination whether the system achieves its intended purpose and objectives and whether development or deployment should proceed.

framework: US NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023)
requirement_paraphrase: Implement post-deployment monitoring plans, including capturing input from users and AI actors, appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery and change management.

framework: US NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023)
requirement_paraphrase: TEVV tasks run throughout the lifecycle; ideally people doing verification and validation are distinct from those doing test and evaluation; deployment-phase TEVV includes system validation, integration testing, recalibration and compliance with legal, regulatory and ethical specifications.

framework: US NIST AI RMF Playbook (AIRC; companion to AI RMF 1.0)
requirement_paraphrase: Suggested actions include testing and evaluating systems in non-optimised conditions, measuring systems before deployment in conditions similar to expected scenarios, measuring validity (false positive/negative rates) and efficiency against ground truth in deployment context, and documenting differences between measurement setting and deployment environment.
who_tests: AI actors with socio-technical, human factors and UI/UX experts

framework: US NIST AI RMF Playbook (AIRC; companion to AI RMF 1.0)
requirement_paraphrase: Suggested actions include stress-testing under likely scenarios and beyond known limits, testing under conditions similar to past incidents, chaos-engineering approaches, and documenting the range of conditions under which the system fails safely.

framework: US NIST AI RMF Playbook (AIRC; companion to AI RMF 1.0)
requirement_paraphrase: Suggested actions include red-team exercises under adversarial or stress conditions, documenting red-team results, and using separate testing teams (set up under GOVERN) so that decisions about AI systems are independent; assess independence and stature of TEVV actors.

framework: US NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile (July 2024)
requirement_paraphrase: Establish minimum thresholds for performance or assurance criteria and review them as part of deployment approval (go/no-go) policies, procedures and processes.

framework: US NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile (July 2024)
requirement_paraphrase: Establish a test plan and response policy, before developing highly capable models, to periodically evaluate whether the model may misuse CBRN information or capabilities and/or offensive cyber capabilities.

framework: US NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile (July 2024)
requirement_paraphrase: Define the use cases and contexts where structured human feedback such as GAI red-teaming is most beneficial; engage in internal and external evaluations, red-teaming and impact assessments with representative AI actors; verify those conducting structured human feedback exercises are not directly involved in developing the same model.
who_tests: Internal and external evaluators not involved in development

framework: US NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile (July 2024)
requirement_paraphrase: Consider baseline benchmark performance when selecting a model; evaluate capability claims with empirically validated methods; share pre-deployment test results with actors holding release approval authority; use a purpose-built testing environment such as NIST Dioptra.

framework: US NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile (July 2024)
requirement_paraphrase: Avoid extrapolating performance from narrow or anecdotal assessments; review and verify sources and citations in outputs during pre-deployment measurement and monitoring; regularly review safety/security guardrails, including reasons the system was initially judged safe to deploy.

framework: US NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile (July 2024)
requirement_paraphrase: Verify the architecture can monitor outputs and recover from errors when security anomalies are detected; verify the system handles inappropriate, malicious or illegal queries properly; regularly evaluate vulnerabilities to circumvention of safety measures.

framework: US NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile (July 2024)
requirement_paraphrase: Perform AI red-teaming to assess resilience to abuse for attacking other systems, generative-AI attacks such as prompt injection, and ML attacks such as adversarial examples, data poisoning, membership inference, model extraction; verify fine-tuning does not compromise safety and security controls.

framework: US NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile (July 2024)
requirement_paraphrase: Conduct AI red-teaming for privacy issues such as output of training data, model extraction, membership inference, revealing confidential or personal information, and tracking user location.
who_tests: Red teams (with TEVV actors and domain experts)

framework: US NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile (July 2024)
requirement_paraphrase: Use use-case-appropriate benchmarks to quantify bias, stereotyping and hateful content, documenting benchmark assumptions and possible train/test contamination; conduct fairness assessments across demographic groups using field testing with sub-groups, red-teaming with counterfactual prompts, and general fairness metrics where outcomes are categorical or numeric.

framework: US NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile (July 2024)
requirement_paraphrase: Create measurement error models for pre-deployment metrics to show construct validity; measure or estimate and document biases or statistical variance in metrics or human feedback processes.
who_tests: TEVV actors and/or domain experts (actor not fully specified)

framework: US NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile (July 2024)
requirement_paraphrase: Conduct adversarial testing at a regular cadence to map and measure GAI risks; evaluate performance in real-world scenarios; verify and document that structured public feedback results are incorporated in deployment go/no-go decisions.

framework: US NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile (July 2024)
requirement_paraphrase: Describes that current pre-deployment TEVV for GAI may be inadequate, non-systematically applied or mismatched to deployment context; anecdotal tests such as standardised exams do not guarantee validity; jailbreak or prompt-engineering tests may not assess validity; laboratory and benchmark settings may not predict real-world impacts.

framework: US NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile (July 2024)
clause_or_page: Appendix A.1.5 Structured Public Feedback, p.49-51
requirement_paraphrase: Describes participatory engagement, field testing and AI red-teaming as structured feedback methods; red-team quality depends on team expertise; diverse, interdisciplinary red teams with domain expertise are suggested; types are general public, expert, combination, and human/AI.
who_tests: Red teams (public, expert, mixed, or AI-assisted)

framework: US NIST AI 800-2 ipd (CAISI) Practices for Automated Benchmark Evaluations of Language Models (Initial Public Draft, January 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Draft provides voluntary preliminary best practices for automated benchmark evaluations of language models and AI agent systems, in three stages: define objectives, implement/run, analyse/report; scoped to existing benchmarks, not creating new ones.

framework: US NIST AI 800-2 ipd (CAISI) Practices for Automated Benchmark Evaluations of Language Models (Initial Public Draft, January 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Select benchmarks that meet the objectives: document what the benchmark measures and verify its relevance to the objective; confirming that a benchmark predicts downstream outcomes of interest is described as emerging practice.

framework: US NIST AI 800-2 ipd (CAISI) Practices for Automated Benchmark Evaluations of Language Models (Initial Public Draft, January 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Design the evaluation protocol, write evaluation code, run and track results, and debug the evaluation; common bugs include degraded serving; evaluation cheating and evaluation awareness are listed as bugs tagged [Emerging Practice].

framework: US NIST AI 800-2 ipd (CAISI) Practices for Automated Benchmark Evaluations of Language Models (Initial Public Draft, January 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Define, conduct and report a statistically valid analysis procedure, ideally defined in advance, that accounts for sources of variation and uncertainty and states assumptions.

framework: US NIST CAISSI program page (nist.gov/caisi; titled 'Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI)' as retrieved 2026-10-16; formerly CAISI)
requirement_paraphrase: The centre states it will develop guidelines and best practices and help industry develop voluntary standards, establish voluntary agreements with private sector SI developers and evaluators, and lead unclassified evaluations of SI capabilities that may pose national security risks, focusing on demonstrable risks such as cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical weapons.

framework: UK AI Playbook for the UK Government (GDS, published 2025-02-10)
requirement_paraphrase: Fully test the product before deployment, have robust assurance and regular checks of the live tool, and provide ways for users to report issues that prompt human review.

framework: UK AI Playbook for the UK Government (GDS, published 2025-02-10)
requirement_paraphrase: Understand how to monitor and mitigate drift, bias and (for generative AI) hallucinations and have a robust testing and monitoring process to catch them.

framework: UK AI Playbook for the UK Government (GDS, published 2025-02-10)
clause_or_page: Ethics > Safety, security and robustness (H3) > Practical recommendations
requirement_paraphrase: Establish performance metrics measuring accuracy of outputs; test the system in a variety of scenarios including extreme or rare events; implement red teaming and record behaviour under unexpected or anomalous scenarios.
who_tests: Not specified (delivery team or red team is an inference)

framework: UK AI Playbook for the UK Government (GDS, published 2025-02-10)
clause_or_page: Using AI safely and responsibly > Ethics (introductory paragraphs after the six themes, before 'Safety, security and robustness')
requirement_paraphrase: Where possible, make specific and robust measurements to assess AI systems, for example evaluating accuracy and output quality against protected characteristics in the Equality Act 2010, choosing assessments suited to the technology and use case.

framework: UK AI Playbook for the UK Government (GDS, published 2025-02-10)
clause_or_page: Ethics > Accountability and responsibility (Practical recommendations and Liability)
requirement_paraphrase: Use assurance techniques to evaluate performance; establish a human-in-the-loop process to oversee and validate outputs in high-impact or high-risk situations; reconsider use if risk is too high; nominate a senior responsible owner.
who_tests: Not specified; senior responsible owner and human reviewers are named

framework: UK AI Playbook for the UK Government (GDS, published 2025-02-10)
requirement_paraphrase: AI services must be secure and resilient and comply with Secure by Design principles and the Government Cyber Security Standard; build safeguards including security testing and, for generative AI, content filtering and validation checks.

framework: UK AI Playbook for the UK Government (GDS, published 2025-02-10)
clause_or_page: Security > Practical recommendations: 'Applies to generative AI' (public-facing LLM chatbots; no automatic destructive or irreversible actions) and 'Applies to AI' (review enterprise access controls before deploying an AI tool)
requirement_paraphrase: Avoid putting LLM chatbots on public-facing government websites unless the risk of direct prompt injection is acceptable for the use case; prevent generative AI responses from automatically triggering destructive or irreversible actions without human review; review enterprise access controls before deploying AI tools.

framework: UK AI Playbook for the UK Government (GDS, published 2025-02-10)
clause_or_page: Data protection and privacy > Accuracy: Practical recommendations
requirement_paraphrase: Test AI outputs against existing knowledge and expertise during training and testing; be transparent that outputs are statistically informed guesses; document sources.

framework: UK AI Playbook for the UK Government (GDS, published 2025-02-10)
clause_or_page: Governance > AI quality assurance (Validation of AI)
requirement_paraphrase: Any update to an AI system must go through a quantitative testing and validation process as part of change control; teams must make sure the products, services and standards they rely on comply with the required standards set by standards development organisations (SDOs) such as ISO.

framework: UK AI Playbook for the UK Government (GDS, published 2025-02-10)
requirement_paraphrase: Once released, keep ongoing performance monitoring with evidence that the system operates as expected; use managed release processes with the ability to withdraw and revert; monitor for model drift.

framework: UK DSIT Introduction to AI assurance (published 2024-02-12)
requirement_paraphrase: Lists a spectrum of assurance mechanisms - risk assessment, impact assessment, bias audit, compliance audit, conformity assessment (often including performance testing), formal verification - to be used in combination across the AI lifecycle, proportionate to risk.
who_tests: Internal teams or third-party assurance providers

framework: UK DSIT Introduction to AI assurance (published 2024-02-12)
requirement_paraphrase: Conformity assessment may include testing, inspection, validation, verification and certification; depending on risk it should be done by an independent third-party body; it is UK government policy that where third-party conformity assessment is sought it should come from a UKAS-accredited organisation.
who_tests: Independent third-party conformity assessment body (UKAS-accredited per policy)

framework: UK AI Security Institute (AISI)
clause_or_page: AI Safety Institute approach to evaluations (published 2024-02-09), sections 'AISI's approach to evaluations'
requirement_paraphrase: AISI conducts pre-deployment and post-deployment evaluations of advanced AI systems using automated capability assessments, expert red-teaming, human uplift studies and AI agent evaluations, focusing on misuse (chemical/biological, cyber), societal impacts, autonomous systems and safeguards.
who_tests: UK AI Security Institute (government), with company cooperation

framework: UK AI Security Institute (AISI)
requirement_paraphrase: AISI states it tests leading AI systems before they are released and collaborates with AI companies, with pre-deployment access to leading models; it open-sources evaluation tools such as Inspect.

framework: UK Frontier AI Safety Commitments (AI Seoul Summit 2024)
requirement_paraphrase: Signatory organisations commit to assess risks of frontier models across the lifecycle, including before deployment, considering results from internal and external evaluations such as independent third-party evaluators and home governments.
who_tests: Signatory developers; independent evaluators/home governments as appropriate

framework: UK Frontier AI Safety Commitments (AI Seoul Summit 2024)
requirement_paraphrase: Set thresholds at which severe risks are intolerable, assess whether thresholds have been breached, articulate mitigations, and follow explicit processes if thresholds are met, in the extreme not developing or deploying a model if mitigations cannot keep risk below thresholds.

framework: UK Frontier AI Safety Commitments (AI Seoul Summit 2024)
clause_or_page: Preamble paragraph on best practices; Commitments VII-VIII
requirement_paraphrase: Signatories affirm internal and external red-teaming for severe and novel threats, publication of capabilities and limits, and public transparency on safety framework implementation, explaining how external actors are involved in assessing risk and adherence.

framework: UK DSIT AI Management Essentials (AIME) tool
requirement_paraphrase: AIME is described as a self-assessment tool to help organisations assess and implement responsible AI management systems and processes.

framework: Singapore IMDA Starter Kit for Testing LLM-Based Applications for Safety and Reliability (v1.0, January 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Set of voluntary guidelines for pre-deployment testing of LLM apps for baseline safety and reliability across five risks: hallucination/inaccuracy, bias in decision making, undesirable content, data leakage, and vulnerability to adversarial prompts.
who_tests: App developer / deployer (self-testing), optionally independent testers

framework: Singapore IMDA Starter Kit for Testing LLM-Based Applications for Safety and Reliability (v1.0, January 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Three-step approach: identify relevant risks and set thresholds; test in a structured manner from outputs to components; analyse results to decide whether thresholds are met. No universal baseline applies; each organisation sets its own.

framework: Singapore IMDA Starter Kit for Testing LLM-Based Applications for Safety and Reliability (v1.0, January 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Run output testing (black-box end-to-end evaluation after components and mitigations are in place, reflecting real user interaction) and component testing (e.g. retrieval step in RAG, filters, system prompt) to locate failure points and catch faults masked by correct outputs.
who_tests: Developers, testing teams, third-party testers, compliance/responsible-AI professionals

framework: Singapore IMDA Starter Kit for Testing LLM-Based Applications for Safety and Reliability (v1.0, January 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Check robustness (varied, perturbed, adversarial phrasing) and consistency (repeat runs); test breadth and depth scaled to stakes, repeating tests and evaluating average, minimum and maximum scores; if resources are limited, either use a subset instead of full benchmarks, or run the full set once and repeat a targeted subset (e.g. borderline prompts).
who_tests: Developers, testing teams, third-party testers, compliance/responsible-AI professionals

framework: Singapore IMDA Starter Kit for Testing LLM-Based Applications for Safety and Reliability (v1.0, January 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Content red teaming probes the app dynamically for blind spots, multi-turn failures and subjective harms; define targeted vs open-ended objectives; use domain experts, AI experts and target end users with diversity; track acceptable response rate, refusal rate and turns-to-unsafe; annotators may be red teamers, independent third parties or LLM judges with human sampling; automated red teaming (e.g. PAIR, Crescendo-style) is an emerging complement.
who_tests: Developers/deployers, domain experts, independent annotators, automated tools

framework: Singapore IMDA Starter Kit for Testing LLM-Based Applications for Safety and Reliability (v1.0, January 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Identify which of the five risks are relevant to the app before testing and prioritise accordingly; even for low-materiality apps run simple tests on a small representative set for basic hygiene.

framework: Singapore IMDA Starter Kit for Testing LLM-Based Applications for Safety and Reliability (v1.0, January 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Set pass thresholds before testing (to avoid moving goalposts) and refine them after testing only on evidence; thresholds are specific to each app and organisation.
who_tests: Developer / deployer (each organisation sets its own threshold)

framework: Singapore IMDA Starter Kit for Testing LLM-Based Applications for Safety and Reliability (v1.0, January 2026)
clause_or_page: s.3.1.4 Hard-gates and comparative thresholds, p.35
requirement_paraphrase: Define hard-gate thresholds for severe harms: zero tolerance in benchmark testing for illegal content such as CSEM or terrorism and high-stakes topics such as self-harm, plus any regulation-mandated thresholds; otherwise use comparative thresholds against human performance, similar apps, the base model, or the previous version.

framework: Singapore IMDA Starter Kit for Testing LLM-Based Applications for Safety and Reliability (v1.0, January 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Litmus is described as a Singapore government service for testing LLM apps of agencies with 1,600 prompts across security, specialised advice, undesirable and political content; default threshold 95 percent safe responses, adjustable; even a single failure in high-stakes hard-gate cases requires investigation.
who_tests: GovTech service used by government agencies

framework: Singapore IMDA Starter Kit for Testing LLM-Based Applications for Safety and Reliability (v1.0, January 2026)
clause_or_page: Overview table p.7; Part 3 step 2 sections 3.2-3.6 (starting pp.37, 52, 62, 73, 82)
requirement_paraphrase: Prescribes risk-specific tests: hallucination (domain knowledge, out-of-domain handling, RAG); bias (parity and counterfactual perturbation tests); undesirable content (type, ease of elicitation, helpfulness/over-refusal); data leakage (type of data, elicitation, system prompt); adversarial prompts (direct and indirect injection).
who_tests: Developers, testing teams, third-party testers, compliance/responsible-AI professionals

framework: Singapore IMDA Starter Kit for Testing LLM-Based Applications for Safety and Reliability (v1.0, January 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Compare results with pre-defined thresholds then review failure cases; adjust thresholds only with documented evidence; break results down by sub-category and attack technique, quantify variance and confidence intervals across runs, and analyse failures qualitatively including faults in the LLM judge.

framework: Singapore IMDA Starter Kit for Testing LLM-Based Applications for Safety and Reliability (v1.0, January 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Re-test after scheduled reviews, on user feedback, and after significant changes such as a new LLM, changed system prompt, architecture or integrations; repeat original benchmarks to check safety impact.

framework: Singapore AI Verify Testing Framework (for traditional and generative AI; updated 2025-05-29)
clause_or_page: Overview (unnumbered, before p.2) of the PDF; mapping, date and audiences from the web page https://aiverifyfoundation.sg/tools/ai-verify-testing-framework/
requirement_paraphrase: Process-check framework to assess AI systems against 11 principles (transparency, explainability, reproducibility, safety, security, robustness, fairness, data governance, accountability, human agency and oversight, inclusive growth); each item has outcome, process and evidence, answered Yes/No/N/A with elaboration; mapped to NIST AI RMF, NIST GenAI Profile, Hiroshima Process code of conduct and ISO/IEC 42001.
who_tests: AI system owner (self-assessment); internal compliance; external auditors may validate

framework: Singapore AI Verify Testing Framework (for traditional and generative AI; updated 2025-05-29)
clause_or_page: Outcome 4.1 / Process 4.1.1, p.29 (technical testing, generative AI)
requirement_paraphrase: Carry out regular safety and harm tests (e.g. hallucination, toxicity) using use-case-appropriate benchmarks and red-teaming, document instructions to red-teamers, test in secure environments at several lifecycle checkpoints and before deployment, have stakeholders decide whether scores are acceptable, and share results.
who_tests: AI system owner with product/risk stakeholders; tools such as Project Moonshot

framework: Singapore AI Verify Testing Framework (for traditional and generative AI; updated 2025-05-29)
requirement_paraphrase: Traditional AI: compute accuracy and compare with and without added noise. Generative AI: benchmark against time or other models and test perturbed prompts (synonyms, typos, punctuation, adversarial perturbation) with the same metric.
who_tests: AI system owner using AI Verify / Moonshot

framework: Singapore AI Verify Testing Framework (for traditional and generative AI; updated 2025-05-29)
requirement_paraphrase: Put a mechanism in place to decide when a changed AI system merits a new technical robustness review; establish a strategy to ensure the system is valid and reliable.

framework: Singapore AI Verify Testing Framework (for traditional and generative AI; updated 2025-05-29)
clause_or_page: Outcome 7.1 / Process 7.1.1, p.71 (technical testing, traditional AI)
requirement_paraphrase: System owner selects fairness metrics for sensitive features and measures disparity of error rates across groups.
who_tests: AI system owner using AI Verify toolkit

framework: Singapore AI Verify Testing Framework (for traditional and generative AI; updated 2025-05-29)
clause_or_page: Outcome 7.2 / Process 7.2.1, p.72 (technical testing, generative AI)
requirement_paraphrase: Test for safety and possible harms against individuals or groups using benchmarks and red-teaming, document red-teamer instructions, and have stakeholders judge score acceptability.
who_tests: AI system owner using Project Moonshot

framework: Singapore AI Verify Testing Framework (for traditional and generative AI; updated 2025-05-29)
clause_or_page: Outcome 2.1 / Process 2.1.1, p.14 (technical testing, traditional AI)
requirement_paraphrase: For each model, run explainability methods to help users understand drivers of the model's output.
who_tests: AI system owner using AI Verify toolkit

framework: Singapore AI Verify Testing Framework (for traditional and generative AI; updated 2025-05-29)
requirement_paraphrase: Assess repeatability by checking whether the model gives consistent outputs for the same input, and reproduce consistent outputs of the system.

framework: Singapore AI Verify Testing Framework (for traditional and generative AI; updated 2025-05-29)
requirement_paraphrase: If using a black-box or third-party model, assess the vendor's claim on accuracy.

framework: Singapore AI Verify Testing Framework (for traditional and generative AI; updated 2025-05-29)
requirement_paraphrase: Assess risks and risk levels per use case; continuously assess, measure and monitor outcomes and risks including after deployment; identify and document TEVV considerations (experimental design, data representativeness, construct validity).

framework: Singapore AI Verify Testing Framework (for traditional and generative AI; updated 2025-05-29)
requirement_paraphrase: Conduct security risk assessments per industry standards; release models or systems only after appropriate security checks and evaluation, including benchmarking and security testing before release and verifying model/data signatures and hashes.

framework: Singapore AI Verify Testing Framework (for traditional and generative AI; updated 2025-05-29)
requirement_paraphrase: Hold a systematic pre-production review presenting performance, explainability and fairness metrics to decision makers; set a frequency (time- or event-based) and process for re-testing deployed systems; keep a strategy for independent oversight of development and deployment.

framework: Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI (IMDA / AI Verify Foundation, published 30 May 2024; PDF file dated 19 June 2024)
clause_or_page: Trusted Development and Deployment dimension, 'Evaluation', p.14 (government-transparency sentence in 'Disclosure', p.14)
requirement_paraphrase: Benchmarking and red teaming are the two main evaluation approaches today but fall far short of a robust assessment (front-end focus, missing tools incl. dangerous-capability tests, poor comparability); the framework calls for a more comprehensive, systematic safety evaluation approach that could include a baseline set of required safety tests developed in consultation with policymakers; the adjacent Disclosure text says greater transparency to government will be needed for potentially high-risk models.

framework: Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (version read: v1.0, 22 Jan 2026; the v1.5 file was not readable)
requirement_paraphrase: Framework gives organisations a structured overview of risks and emerging best practice for deploying AI agents; before deployment organisations should test agents for baseline safety and reliability including execution accuracy, policy adherence and tool use; roll out gradually with continuous monitoring after deployment.

framework: Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (version read: v1.0, 22 Jan 2026; v1.5 not read)
requirement_paraphrase: Test agents for safety and security before deployment, covering overall task execution, policy compliance (including routing for human approval), tool calling (right tool, permissions, inputs, order) and robustness to errors and edge cases; test entire workflows including reasoning and tool calls, and multi-agent systems.

framework: Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (version read: v1.0, 22 Jan 2026; v1.5 not read)
requirement_paraphrase: Test in real or realistic environments that mirror production (balancing realism against risk of real-world side effects), test repeatedly across varied datasets to observe low-probability behaviours and stability, and evaluate results at scale using different methods per workflow part; the source describes current industry solutions as LLM or agent evaluators, or human evaluation (practice described, not a recommendation).

framework: Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (version read: v1.0, 22 Jan 2026; v1.5 not read)
requirement_paraphrase: Roll out gradually (by users, tools, systems exposed), continuously monitor and log agent behaviour with failsafes and real-time intervention, audit at regular intervals, define alert thresholds, and keep testing after deployment for model drift and changes.

framework: Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (v1.5, published 2026-05-20, updated 2026-06-05)
clause_or_page: s.2.3.2 'Before deploying, test agents', case study box 'Google x Singapore Government: Testing computer use agents', p.40 (v1.5)
requirement_paraphrase: Case study (descriptive): Google, CSA, GovTech and IMDA ran a sandbox testing computer-use agents for three potential public-sector uses (automated QA of government digital services, automated AI safety testing of third-party chatbots, social assistance applications). Lessons: use realistic test data and environments; log and evaluate the agent's reasoning at each step; identify use-case-specific attack vectors such as indirect prompt injection; keep humans in the loop during testing. Findings: the agent included extraneous personal details in a significant number of cases and in some instances navigated to arbitrary URLs when instructed by injected content.

framework: Singapore Cataloguing LLM Evaluations (IMDA / AI Verify Foundation discussion draft, October 2023)
clause_or_page: Introduction para 4(c), p.4; Part 3 paras 39-42, p.22 (Part 3 spans pp.22-28)
requirement_paraphrase: Recommends a baseline of pre-deployment evaluations that LLMs should minimally be tested on regardless of use case: bias, factuality, toxicity generation, robustness and data governance, described as a policy position.

framework: EU AI Act (Reg. (EU) 2024/1689, as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744)
requirement_paraphrase: Sandboxes give a controlled environment for development, training, testing and validation under an agreed sandbox plan; authorities give guidance and supervision to identify risks, and on request supply written proof and an exit report which market surveillance authorities and notified bodies must take positively into account.

framework: EU AI Act (Reg. (EU) 2024/1689, as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744)
requirement_paraphrase: Providers or prospective providers of Annex III systems, or systems covered by Annex I Section A legislation, may test in real-world conditions outside sandboxes at any time before market placement, alone or with deployers.

framework: EU AI Act - GPAI Code of Practice (Safety and Security chapter)

clause_or_page: s.2.3.3 'When deploying, continuously monitor and test', case study 'GovTech: Phased rollouts of coding assistants', pp.42-43
requirement_paraphrase: Case study: GovTech (statutory board) rolled out agentic coding assistants (Windsurf, GitHub Copilot Agent Mode from Oct 2025; Claude Code from Apr 2026) after extensive tests on failure and threat vectors such as agent manipulation, hallucination and MCP server compromise and after implementing controls; phase 1 limited to GovTech employees, no MCP access and low-risk systems; before phase 2 (other agencies, then vendors) red teaming was conducted to validate guardrails, with central logging and a sandboxed MCP governance path.

framework: Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (v1.5, published 2026-05-20, updated 2026-06-05)
clause_or_page: s.2.3 overview p.33 and s.2.3.3 'Robust change management', p.45
requirement_paraphrase: Throughout the lifecycle implement change management and version control; define triggers that start a change review (technical e.g. model updates or tool changes; environmental; performance e.g. anomalous behaviour; regulatory) and categorise changes by risk, with lighter review for minor prompt refinements, full governance review for material changes such as model updates or autonomy adjustments, and possibly an immediate re-risk assessment for critical changes affecting high-stakes decisions.

framework: South Korea - Enforcement Decree of the AI Framework Act (Presidential Decree No. 36053, 21 Jan 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: The impact assessment of high-impact AI must cover: affected persons/groups; affected fundamental rights; content and scope of social and economic impacts; usage patterns; quantitative and qualitative metrics and methods used; measures to prevent and mitigate risks and recover losses; and, where needed, an improvement plan. The operator may conduct it itself or commission a third party; the Minister notifies other matters.

framework: China - TC260-PG-20268A Cybersecurity Standard Practice Guide: AI Application Security Guidelines, General (v1.0-202609, TC260 Secretariat, Sep 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: In the verification and validation stage, organisations validate against set reliability, fairness, transparency and explainability metrics; run security tests (manual, automated, cross-validation) by application type: generated-content safeguards; collision and stability for physical devices; explainability, transparency, robustness and backdoor risks for major decisions; protections for minors and special groups. If results fall short, improve (e.g., model tuning) and retest until requirements are met, or redesign.
who_tests: Organisations deploying AI applications; may serve as reference for regulators and third-party testing bodies (Sec. 1)

framework: China - TC260-PG-20268A Cybersecurity Standard Practice Guide: AI Application Security Guidelines, General (v1.0-202609, TC260 Secretariat, Sep 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: At deployment, use safety guardrails to identify and block illegal content, prevent prompt injection and runaway execution chains; where third-party protection services are used, test and evaluate their security capability and service continuity; perform security checks on hardware, software and third-party tools, fix known vulnerabilities or mitigate, and track vulnerabilities to prevent supply-chain backdoors.

framework: NCA 'Draft of AI Cybersecurity Guidelines' (AICG-1:2026), draft for public consultation (closed 5 Aug 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Conduct a cybersecurity risk assessment that classifies AI agents' actions by potential impact, likelihood and reversibility, and apply appropriate safeguards.

framework: NCA 'Draft of AI Cybersecurity Guidelines' (AICG-1:2026), draft for public consultation (closed 5 Aug 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Continuously assess the cybersecurity capabilities and resilience of AI agents throughout the development lifecycle.

framework: NCA 'Draft of AI Cybersecurity Guidelines' (AICG-1:2026), draft for public consultation (closed 5 Aug 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Develop guardrails to detect and prevent malicious input, unauthorised actions and sensitive information disclosure, and ensure they are tested before production use and after material changes.

framework: NCA 'Draft of AI Cybersecurity Guidelines' (AICG-1:2026), draft for public consultation (closed 5 Aug 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: Assess and manage the cybersecurity of third-party AI components in AI systems before use and on an ongoing basis.

framework: NCA 'Draft of AI Cybersecurity Guidelines' (AICG-1:2026), draft for public consultation (closed 5 Aug 2026)
requirement_paraphrase: When a vulnerability is detected, disable or restrict vulnerable AI features until remediation is validated.

framework: SFDA MDS-G010 Guidance on AI and ML technologies based Medical Devices (v1.0, 29/11/2022)
requirement_paraphrase: For MDMA the manufacturer is expected to provide technical documentation including product verification and validation; documentation should show verification against design specifications, validation that the device performs as intended, a usability study, and validation of safe performance under normal and reasonably foreseeable abnormal conditions.

framework: SFDA MDS-G010 Guidance on AI and ML technologies based Medical Devices (v1.0, 29/11/2022)
requirement_paraphrase: Manufacturers need to show valid clinical association, analytical/technical validation and clinical validation; clinical validation follows analytical validation, applies to all risk classes, and is evaluated before market placement and after; example metrics include sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV.

framework: SFDA MDS-G010 Guidance on AI and ML technologies based Medical Devices (v1.0, 29/11/2022)
requirement_paraphrase: Where independent review is needed, the clinical evaluation should as far as possible be reviewed by someone not significantly involved in development and with nothing to gain, proportionate to risk; an evaluation based on a comparator device must show clinical and technical equivalence including the algorithm.

framework: SFDA MDS-G010 Guidance on AI and ML technologies based Medical Devices (v1.0, 29/11/2022)
requirement_paraphrase: Analytical validation should use a large independent reference dataset reflecting the intended population (prevalence, multi-centre sourcing, demographics, justified size, not publicly available); performance should be shown to generalise through multisite investigation and subgroup analysis, and be tested against a gold standard.

framework: SFDA MDS-G010 Guidance on AI and ML technologies based Medical Devices (v1.0, 29/11/2022)
requirement_paraphrase: Effects should be evaluated in clinically relevant conditions integrated into the clinical workflow, comparing clinicians with and without the device; manufacturers should locally validate devices developed and approved in other jurisdictions.

framework: SFDA MDS-G010 Guidance on AI and ML technologies based Medical Devices (v1.0, 29/11/2022)
requirement_paraphrase: Because AI/ML devices can learn continuously, manufacturers are required to use post-market continuous monitoring of safety, effectiveness and performance in real-world settings.

framework: SFDA MDS-G010 Guidance on AI and ML technologies based Medical Devices (v1.0, 29/11/2022)
requirement_paraphrase: Manufacturers are required (per MDS-REQ 1) to show no unacceptable risk and that benefits outweigh residual risk; safety requirements should include evaluation results on algorithm limitations and performance; a risk management review per ISO 14971:2019 Clause 9 should be performed before commercial release.

framework: SFDA MDS-G010 Guidance on AI and ML technologies based Medical Devices (v1.0, 29/11/2022)
requirement_paraphrase: SFDA is to be informed via GHAD of significant changes within 10 days; the manufacturer shall have QMS procedures for change control, and all changes shall be evaluated, verified and validated under those procedures.

framework: SDAIA AI Service Provider Accreditation (National Data Governance Platform service)
requirement_paraphrase: AI software and service providers register, appoint an AI officer, and complete a per-product questionnaire with supporting files on adherence to AI ethics standards; after committee review the product receives an incentive label and the provider an accreditation certificate.

framework: SDAIA AI Ethics Self-Assessment tool (National Data Governance Platform service)
requirement_paraphrase: Tool for entities to compare their current practice against defined standards and obtain the level of ethical compliance of an AI model; links to the AI Ethics Principles.

framework: UAE National Cyber Security Policy for Artificial Intelligence, Version 1.1 (UAE Cyber Security Council, November 2025; v1.0 September 2025)
clause_or_page: Implementation Guidance 3.4.4 'Testing and Validation of AI/ML Systems', printed p.36
requirement_paraphrase: The entity should keep a framework for testing and validating AI/ML systems so accuracy, reliability and performance meet defined criteria; all AI/ML systems should be rigorously tested before deployment for functionality, security and resilience, covering varied scenarios and edge cases.
who_tests: The entity (federal ministries and authorities; non-government CII entities; emirate government entities per s1.2)

framework: UAE National Cyber Security Policy for Artificial Intelligence, Version 1.1 (UAE Cyber Security Council, November 2025; v1.0 September 2025)
clause_or_page: Implementation Guidance 3.1.4 (Change Management), printed p.21; 3.2.3 (Patch Management), printed p.24
requirement_paraphrase: Manual changes to AI/ML models, algorithms, training data or configurations should be documented, reviewed, approved and tested in a secure environment before deployment, with a rollback plan where possible; patches and updates should be tested in a controlled environment before production.
who_tests: The entity (federal ministries and authorities; non-government CII entities; emirate government entities per s1.2)

framework: DoH Abu Dhabi Responsible AI Risk Management Protocol (ref. as extracted DoH/Protocol/DDGO/RALRM/V1/2025, V1, published and effective Oct 2025, revision Oct 2028)
clause_or_page: s3 Recommended Protocol, Risk Evaluation and Treatment, Step 4 'Control Identification', printed p.6
requirement_paraphrase: Risk controls for AI systems are identified through review of safeguards, gap analysis and stakeholder consultation, and are tested through simulations or pilot studies before full implementation to confirm they reduce risk and support AI safety and reliability.
who_tests: Product owner / risk owner in DoH units and licensed Abu Dhabi healthcare entities; DoH (DDGO) reviews

framework: DoH Abu Dhabi Responsible AI Risk Management Protocol (ref. as extracted DoH/Protocol/DDGO/RALRM/V1/2025, V1, published and effective Oct 2025, revision Oct 2028)
clause_or_page: s3 Risk Assessment, Steps 1-3 (asset criticality, likelihood, impact, risk calculation), printed pp.4-6
requirement_paraphrase: Sets a risk rating method for AI use cases: asset criticality on four levels (e.g. clinical decision support high, surgical robot very high), threat likelihood and impact on 1-5 scales, exposure factor = likelihood x impact, risk rating = criticality x exposure; medium and high risks need treatment and very high risks shall be avoided.
who_tests: Product owner / risk owner in DoH units and licensed Abu Dhabi healthcare entities; DoH (DDGO) reviews

framework: DoH Abu Dhabi Responsible AI Risk Management Protocol (ref. as extracted DoH/Protocol/DDGO/RALRM/V1/2025, V1, published and effective Oct 2025, revision Oct 2028)
clause_or_page: Decision Point DP1 (Residual Risk Rating), printed p.6; Step 6 'Avoid High Risk System', printed p.7
requirement_paraphrase: AI systems with very high residual risk must not be implemented. Step 6, reached for very high risk, says a system classified as high risk despite existing controls must be avoided, while DP1 routes high and medium risks to mitigation (Step 7).
who_tests: Product owner / risk owner in DoH units and licensed Abu Dhabi healthcare entities; DoH (DDGO) reviews

framework: DoH Abu Dhabi Responsible AI Risk Management Protocol (ref. as extracted DoH/Protocol/DDGO/RALRM/V1/2025, V1, published and effective Oct 2025, revision Oct 2028)
clause_or_page: Step 10 (10.1, 10.2) Reassessment, printed p.8; Step 11 (11.1, 11.2) Review and Consultation, printed pp.8-9; KPI table p.11
requirement_paraphrase: Risk assessments shall be reviewed at planned intervals and on significant change, and control effectiveness shall be assessed regularly with verified corrective actions. Organisations report risk assessments, incidents and audit findings to DoH; DoH review of high-risk AI systems may include compliance audits, and DoH reviews the risk register. KPIs include an annual AI ethical incident rate threshold below 15%.
who_tests: Product owner / risk owner in DoH units and licensed Abu Dhabi healthcare entities; DoH (DDGO) reviews

framework: DIFC Data Protection Regulations, proposed amendments (Annex A 'Proposed Changes' to DIFCA Consultation Paper No. 3, June 2026; draft cover 'Consolidated Version No. 3, in force on [XX 2026]'; NOT enacted as seen on 2026-10-16)
clause_or_page: Proposed Reg. 10.3.2(b), Annex A printed p.13 (current 10.3.2(b) would become 10.3.2(c))
requirement_paraphrase: Proposed: no one may use, operate or offer for commercial use a System that processes personal data unless the System has been tested for safety verification, including native regulatory and security design (in addition to human-defined purposes and design compliance with Reg. 10.3.1 and Commissioner audit, governance or certification requirements).

framework: DIFC Data Protection Regulations, proposed amendments (Annex A 'Proposed Changes' to DIFCA Consultation Paper No. 3, June 2026; draft cover 'Consolidated Version No. 3, in force on [XX 2026]'; NOT enacted as seen on 2026-10-16)
clause_or_page: Proposed Reg. 10.3.1(f) 'Safety', Annex A printed p.13; Consultation Paper para 18(b) and Q2
requirement_paraphrase: Proposed new design concept: a System must be designed, developed and operated with safeguards to identify use of personal data, assess and mitigate risks of harm to individuals, and prevent discriminatory or biased outcomes through appropriate oversight, testing and controls.
who_tests: Not specified (Systems developed and used in products or services affecting Data Subjects)

framework: DIFC Data Protection Regulations, proposed amendments (Annex A 'Proposed Changes' to DIFCA Consultation Paper No. 3, June 2026; draft cover 'Consolidated Version No. 3, in force on [XX 2026]'; NOT enacted as seen on 2026-10-16)
clause_or_page: Proposed Reg. 10.2.2(b)(vi), Annex A printed pp.10-11
requirement_paraphrase: Proposed: where no applicable codes, certifications or policy frameworks exist for the System type, the notice must describe the privacy-by-design and default measures taken; the Commissioner and any advisory body may then request an impact assessment or convene a review and audit body to give technical and governance recommendations.
who_tests: Deployers and Operators (and any person making a System available commercially) in the DIFC; Commissioner of Data Protection; review and audit body convened by the Commissioner
